CHICAGO — The bispecific antibody linvoseltamab exhibited rapid clinical activity among patients with relapsed or refractory systemic light chain amyloidosis, according to phase 1/phase 2 trial results presented at ASCO Annual Meeting. All 20 treated patients achieved objective response and 18 achieved hematologic complete response. Data derived from Wechalekar AD, et al. Abstract 7502. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. Linvoseltamab (Lynozyfic, Regeneron) also exhibited what researchers characterized as a manageable safety profile, with no dose-limiting toxicities reported. Hans C. Lee “The safety profile is very encouraging, and to see rapid and deep hematologic responses is unprecedented in this patient population,” Hans C. Lee, MD, director of myeloma research at Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told Healio. “This could have tremendous implications for previously treated light chain amyloidosis — and possibly down the road for newly diagnosed patients.” ‘Significant unmet need’ Light chain (AL) amyloidosis — a rare systemic plasma cell disorder — results in pathogenic secretion of light chain fibrils that gather in organs such as the heart or kidneys. This can lead to end-organ damage, other significant morbidity or death. Approximately 43% of all patients with AL amyloidosis survive 5 years and about 27% live 10 years. The CD38-targeted antibody daratumumab (Darzalex, Johson & Johnson) in combination with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone is approved for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis. However, no therapies are approved for relapsed or refractory disease; consequently, drugs that are efficacious for treatment of multiple myeloma often are used off-label. “Oftentimes these approaches do not lead to rapid and deep responses,” Lee said. “We are trying to target plasma cells effectively, but it also is imperative to decrease the production and organ deposition of the light chain fibrils as quickly as possible, so there is a significant unmet need in this setting.” Linvoseltamab, a bispecific B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CD3 T-cell engager, is approved for treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma who received at least four previous therapies. In the LINKER-AL2 trial, Lee and colleagues assessed the safety and efficacy of linvoseltamab monotherapy for patients with relapsed or refractory systemic AL amyloidosis. ‘Encouraged and excited’ Trial participants received step-up doses of IV linvoseltamab — 5 mg on day 1 and 25 mg on day 8 — of cycle 0. They received full subcutaneous doses — either 80 mg or 240 mg — once weekly for two 28-day cycles, followed by once every 4 weeks in cycles 3 through 12. Dose-limiting toxicities within 28 days of the first full dose served as the primary endpoint of the phase 1 portion of the trial. Secondary endpoints included hematologic complete response — assessed by free light chain ratio and absence of amyloidogenic light chains — along with rates of objective response, very good partial response or better, and time to response. Investigators also evaluated additional safety outcomes. Twenty patients (median age, 64 years) — 60% of whom had received prior daratumumab — received treatment. Seven received 80 mg full doses and 13 received 240 mg doses. Median follow-up reached 9.5 weeks. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred. All patients experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, and 65% experienced grade 3 or higher events. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events — which occurred primarily during step-up dosing — included cytokine release syndrome (grade 1, 35%; grade 2, 15%) and infusion-related reactions (35%, all grade 1/grade 2). Twenty-five percent of patients developed grade 3 or higher infections. One patient developed grade 1 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. Researchers reported one case of grade 5 ventricular fibrillation in a patient with pre-existing coronary artery disease in the context of coronary artery stent placement, and one case of grade 5 sudden cardiac death in a patient with cardiac amyloidosis. Investigators deemed both events unrelated to linvoseltamab. “These patients often are quite frail because they have organ involvement, so the safety profile overall is very encouraging,” Lee said. All 20 patients achieved very good partial response or better. Eighteen patients (90%) achieved hematologic complete response. Median time to complete hematologic response was about 1.5 months, and median time to normalization of involved free light chain — defined as less than 20 mg/L — was 15 days. This translated into what Lee called “encouraging organ responses,” with a 73% renal response rate and 50% cardiac response rate. Investigators expect these responses could deepen with longer follow-up, he added. Due to the encouraging phase 1 results, researchers will move forward with the phase 2 portion of the LINKER-AL2 trial. A larger cohort of patients with relapsed or refractory AL amyloidosis will be enrolled and randomly assigned to linvoseltamab at either the 80 mg or 240 mg dose. That study will have “potential registrational intent,” Lee said. “We are encouraged and excited by the efficacy results so far,” Lee said. “They highlight how BCMA bispecific antibodies will be an important modality of therapy for this patient population moving forward. Because this is an off-the-shelf therapy, it can be accessible to patients regardless of whether they are treated at large urban centers or smaller community practices.” For more information: Hans C. Lee, MD, can be reached at hans.lee@scri.com. Published by: Sources/Disclosures Source: Wechalekar AD, et al. Abstract 7502. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. Reference: Habib MH, et al. J Clin Med . 2024;doi:10.3390/jcm13071991 . Disclosures: Regeneron funded this study.
